questions.text: Let X be a recursive language and Y be a recursively enumerable but not recursive language. Let W and Z be two languages such that [latex]\bar{Y}[/latex]  reduces to W, and Z reduces to [latex]\bar{X}[/latex] (reduction means the standard many-one-reduction). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Y is RE but not recursive, so [latex]\bar Y[/latex] is not RE. Since [latex]\bar Y[/latex] reduces to W, W cannot be RE (otherwise [latex]\bar Y[/latex] would be).
- X is recursive, so [latex]\bar X[/latex] is recursive. Z reduces to [latex]\bar X[/latex], so Z is recursive.

Answer: W is not recursively enumerable and Z is recursive

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: W can be recursively enumerable and Z is recursive.
W can be recursive and Z is recursively enumerable
W is not recursively enumerable and Z is recursive
W is not recursively enumerable and Z is not recursive.

questions.text:
Consider the transition diagram of a PDA given below with input alphabet [latex]\Sigma [/latex]={a,b} and stack alphabet [latex]\Gamma[/latex]={X,Z}. Z is the initial stack symbol. Let L denote the language accepted by the PDA.

Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.solution:
The PDA pushes an X for every a in the start state (which is final), then pops one X per b, and accepts when only Z is left.
So [latex]L=\{a^n\mid n\ge0\}\cup\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge1\}[/latex], and every move is deterministic [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] L is a deterministic CFL.

Answer: L is deterministic context-free

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: [latex]L=\{a^{n}b^{n}|n\geq 0\}[/latex] is not accepted by any finite automata
[latex]L=\{a^{n}|n\geq 0\}\cup \{a^{n}b^{n}|n\geq 0\}[/latex] is not accepted by any deterministic PDA
L is not accepted by any Turing machine that halts one very input

questions.text:
Consider the following context-free grammars:

G1: S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]aS|B,
B[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b|bB
G2: S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]aA|bB,
A[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]aA|B|[latex]\varepsilon[/latex],
B[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]bB|[latex]\varepsilon[/latex]

Which one of the following pair of languages is generated by G1 and G2, respectively?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- G1: [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid B[/latex], [latex]B\rightarrow b\mid bB[/latex] gives [latex]a^*b^+[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m\ge0,\ n \gt 0\}[/latex].
- G2: aA gives [latex]a^+b^*[/latex] and bB gives [latex]b^+[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m \gt 0\text{ or }n \gt 0\}[/latex].

Answer: Option 4

questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language: the set of all binary strings having two consecutive 0s and two consecutive 1s?
questions.solution:
The string must contain "00" somewhere and "11" somewhere, in either order:
[latex](0+1)^*\big(00(0+1)^*11+11(0+1)^*00\big)(0+1)^*[/latex] True

- Option 1 forces 00 and 11 to be adjacent (0011 or 1100).
- Option 3 needs only one of them.
- Option 4 forces them at the very start and end.

Answer: Option 2

questions.text:
Which of the following decision problems are undecidable?
I. Given NFAs N1 and N2, is L(N1)[latex]\cap[/latex]L(N2) = [latex]\phi[/latex]?
II. Given a CFG G = (N,[latex]\Sigma [/latex],P,S) and a string [latex]x \in\Sigma ^*[/latex], does [latex]x \in[/latex] L(G)?
III. Given CFGs G1 and G2, is L(G1) = L(G2)?
IV. Given a TM M, is L(M) = [latex]\phi[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: NFA intersection emptiness: build the product automaton and check reachability [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.
- II: CFG membership: CYK algorithm [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.
- III: equivalence of two CFGs [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable.
- IV: emptiness of a TM's language (Rice) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable.

Answer: III and IV only
